Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

MOSCOW, Russia (CNN)  -- A passenger jet caught fire early Sunday, exploded and crashed into railway tracks in the central Russian city of Perm, killing all 88 people on board. Wreckage from the Aeroflot-Nord Boeing 737, which crashed near Perm, lies across a railway track. The exact cause of the pre-dawn crash is under investigation, but government spokesman Vladimir Markin said "a technical breakdown" was a likely cause. Markin said in televised remarks that the failure of one of the Boeing 737-500's two engines may have caused the plane to come down, The Associated Press reported. Airline officials have said there is no indication of terrorism. "We think it's very doubtful that it was the result of a terrorist attack, because at the scene, there were no traces of explosives as we know for now," said Lev Koshlyakov, Deputy Director General of Aeroflot. It took firefighters more than two hours to extinguish the blazing wreckage. When the sun rose, pieces of the Aeroflot jet were strewn about the railroad tracks. "It slammed in front of my house, and there was a huge flame," an unidentified woman in Perm told Russian state television. "It looked like fireworks." She said the impact of the crash "threw me across my sheets.... Then my daughter ran in from the next room and asked if a war had started." She and other witnesses said they saw the aircraft burning before it came crashing down. "It looked like a comet," she said. The jet was en route to Perm from Moscow when the pilots lost communication with air traffic control just before landing about 3:10 a.m. (2110 GMT), an Aeroflot official said. He described the weather at the time as "mediocre." The public safety minister for the Perm region said investigators were combing a 2.5-mile (4-kilometer) area, including homes and railways.  Watch more about the crash » . "Right now, it's apparent that there was a fire on the plane at one kilometer in the air," Yuri Orlov said. "After that, all contact was cut off -- the plane exploded." The flight data recorder has been recovered and will be analyzed by the International Aviation Commission, Russian Transport Minister Igor Levitin said. The plane carried 82 passengers, including seven children, and a crew of six. At least 21 non-Russians were on board, including passport-holders from Azerbaijan, Germany, France, Italy, Switzerland and Ukraine, said Lev Koshlyakov, Aeroflot's deputy director general. The U.S. Embassy confirmed that no Americans were on board the flight, even though one passenger was listed as a U.S. citizen. It is the second crash in the region involving a Boeing 737 in less than a month. An Iran-bound Boeing 737 with 90 people on board crashed on August 24 just outside the airport in Kyrgyzstan's capital, Bishkek, killing 68. The 737 is a workhorse of the airline industry, with thousands of planes in service. Aeroflot said the one that crashed in Perm was manufactured in 1992 and was operated by its Aeroflot-Nord subsidiary. "This Boeing 737 has all the necessary certificates," Koshlyakov said. "We conduct audits and inspections of all the affiliate companies we work with in the realm of their effectiveness, safety and reliability of the airplanes." Airline safety in Russia and the former Soviet Union is among the worst in the world. Aviation experts say poor maintenance, inadequate pilot training and weak government controls are major factors. But Aeroflot is considered one of the safer airlines in the region. Sunday's crash is the first fatal accident for the airline since 1994, when a Russian pilot handed control of an Airbus to his 15-year-old son. It crashed, killing all 75 people on board. Russia's government has now ordered an inquiry into the latest incident, to find out how another routine flight could have ended in tragedy. The National Transportation Safety Board will send a team of investigators to Perm to look into the incident -- a standard practice when a U.S.-made aircraft crashes. CNN's Kathleen Koch and Michael Sefanov contributed to this report .

The precise cause of the pre-dawn crash remains under investigation, though government spokesman Vladimir Markin indicated that "a technical breakdown" was the likely culprit. She recounted that the force of the crash "threw me across my sheets.... Then my daughter ran in from the next room and asked if a war had started." She and other witnesses reported seeing the aircraft ablaze before it plunged to the ground. "It looked like a comet," she said.

The jet was traveling from Moscow to Perm when pilots lost communication with air traffic control just before landing, at approximately 3:10 a.m. (2110 GMT), according to an Aeroflot official, who described weather conditions at the time as "mediocre."

The public safety minister for the Perm region reported that investigators were combing a 2.5-mile (4-kilometer) area, including residential zones and railway lines. "It is now apparent that there was a fire on the plane at an altitude of one kilometer," said Yuri Orlov. "After that, all contact was lost -- the plane exploded."

The flight data recorder has since been recovered and will be analyzed by the International Aviation Commission, according to Russian Transport Minister Igor Levitin.

The aircraft was carrying 82 passengers -- including seven children -- along with a crew of six. At least 21 foreign nationals were aboard, including passport holders from Azerbaijan, Germany, France, Italy, Switzerland, and Ukraine, said Koshlyakov. The U.S. Embassy confirmed that no Americans were on the flight, despite one passenger having been listed as a U.S. citizen.

This marks the second crash involving a Boeing 737 in the region within less than a month. On August 24, an Iran-bound Boeing 737 carrying 90 people crashed just outside the airport in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, killing 68.

The 737 remains a mainstay of the airline industry, with thousands currently in service worldwide. Aeroflot confirmed that the aircraft involved in the Perm crash was manufactured in 1992 and operated by its subsidiary, Aeroflot-Nord. "This Boeing 737 has all the necessary certifications," Koshlyakov said. "We conduct audits and inspections of all affiliate companies we work with, evaluating the effectiveness, safety, and reliability of their aircraft."

Airline safety across Russia and the former Soviet Union remains among the poorest in the world, with aviation experts citing inadequate maintenance, insufficient pilot training, and weak government oversight as major contributing factors. Sunday's crash marks the airline's first fatal accident since 1994, when a Russian pilot allowed his 15-year-old son to take the controls of an Airbus, resulting in a crash that killed all 75 people aboard.

The Russian government has since ordered a formal inquiry into the latest incident to determine how a routine flight could have ended in tragedy. The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board will also dispatch a team of investigators to Perm -- standard procedure whenever a U.S.-manufactured aircraft is involved in a crash.

# Fatal Plane Crash in Perm Claims 88 Lives

**MOSCOW, Russia (CNN)** — Early Sunday morning, a commercial aircraft burst into flames, exploded mid-air, and came down onto railroad tracks in Perm, a city in central Russia, killing everyone aboard—88 people in total. Debris from the destroyed Boeing 737, operated by Aeroflot-Nord, was scattered across the rail lines near the crash site.

Investigators have yet to determine precisely what caused the pre-dawn disaster, though government spokesman Vladimir Markin suggested a mechanical failure was the probable culprit. According to remarks he made on television, cited by The Associated Press, one of the aircraft's two engines may have malfunctioned, triggering the crash.

Aeroflot representatives have dismissed terrorism as a likely explanation. Deputy Director General Lev Koshlyakov stated, "We think it's very doubtful that it was the result of a terrorist attack, because at the scene, there were no traces of explosives as we know for now."

Emergency crews battled the fire for over two hours before bringing it under control. By daybreak, wreckage from the jet covered the railway tracks.

A local resident, speaking to Russian state television without giving her name, described the terrifying scene: "It slammed in front of my house, and there was a huge flame. It looked like fireworks." She recounted being thrown from her bed by the force of the impact, and how her daughter rushed in asking whether war had broken out. Multiple witnesses reported seeing the plane ablaze before it struck the ground, with the woman comparing its appearance to "a comet."

According to an Aeroflot representative, the flight had departed Moscow bound for Perm when contact with air traffic controllers was lost roughly at 3:10 a.m. local time (2110 GMT), shortly before its scheduled landing. He characterized weather conditions at the time as "mediocre."

Yuri Orlov, the Perm region's public safety minister, reported that search teams were examining a zone spanning roughly 2.5 miles (4 kilometers), encompassing residential areas and rail corridors. "Right now, it's apparent that there was a fire on the plane at one kilometer in the air," he explained. "After that, all contact was cut off—the plane exploded."

Russian Transport Minister Igor Levitin announced that the flight data recorder had been recovered and would be examined by the International Aviation Commission.

The flight carried 82 passengers—among them seven children—plus six crew members. Koshlyakov noted that at least 21 foreign nationals were aboard, holding passports from Azerbaijan, Germany, France, Italy, Switzerland, and Ukraine. Although one passenger had been listed as an American citizen, the U.S. Embassy confirmed no Americans were actually on the flight.

This marks the second Boeing 737 crash in the region within the span of a month. On August 24, a Boeing 737 heading to Iran crashed near the airport in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan's capital, killing 68 of the 90 people aboard.

The 737 remains one of the aviation industry's most widely used aircraft models, with thousands currently in operation worldwide. Aeroflot confirmed that the plane involved in the Perm crash dated back to 1992 and was flown by its subsidiary carrier, Aeroflot-Nord. "This Boeing 737 has all the necessary certificates," Koshlyakov affirmed, adding that the airline regularly audits its affiliate carriers to verify safety standards and operational reliability.

Russia and other former Soviet nations continue to rank among the world's worst regions for aviation safety, with experts pointing to substandard maintenance practices, insufficient pilot training, and lax regulatory oversight as key contributing factors. Aeroflot, however, has generally maintained a reputation as one of the region's more reliable carriers. This latest tragedy represents the airline's first fatal incident since 1994, when a pilot allowed his 15-year-old son to take the controls of an Airbus, resulting in a crash that killed all 75 passengers and crew.

Russian authorities have launched a formal investigation to determine how what should have been a routine flight ended in catastrophe. Additionally, the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board plans to dispatch investigators to the crash site—standard protocol whenever an American-manufactured aircraft is involved in an accident.

*CNN's Kathleen Koch and Michael Sefanov contributed to this report.*

# All 88 Aboard Killed as Aeroflot-Nord Boeing 737 Crashes Near Perm, Russia

**PERM, Russia (CNN)** — A Boeing 737-500 operated by Aeroflot-Nord crashed early Sunday while attempting to land at Perm's Bolshoye Savino Airport, killing all 88 people on board in one of Russia's deadliest aviation disasters in recent years, officials said.

Flight 821, traveling from Moscow to Perm, went down around 5:10 a.m. local time, crashing onto a railway line on the outskirts of the city and bursting into flames. Russian emergency officials confirmed that all 82 passengers and six crew members died in the crash.

## Eyewitness Accounts Describe Fiery Scene

Residents living near the crash site described a harrowing scene as the aircraft went down in the early morning darkness.

"I heard a loud roar, like nothing I'd ever heard before, and then a huge explosion," one nearby resident told local reporters. "The sky lit up orange. We ran outside and could see the flames from our yard."

Another witness who lives close to the railway embankment where the wreckage came to rest said the ground shook from the impact.

"There was debris scattered everywhere, across the tracks and into the field," the witness said. "It happened so fast. By the time anyone could get close, the fire had already spread across most of the wreckage."

Emergency crews arriving at the scene reportedly found the aircraft broken into several large sections, with fire crews working for hours to extinguish the flames amid difficult terrain.

## Investigation Underway

Russian aviation authorities said an investigation into the cause of the crash was launched immediately, with the country's Interstate Aviation Committee dispatching a team to examine the wreckage and recover the plane's flight data and cockpit voice recorders.

Officials with Russia's Federal Air Transport Agency said early theories being examined included pilot error, mechanical failure, and adverse weather conditions, though they cautioned that no definitive cause had been established.

"We are looking at all possibilities," a transport ministry spokesperson said in a briefing Sunday. "Nothing will be ruled out until the flight recorders have been fully analyzed."

Local reports indicated that the pilot may have been experiencing spatial disorientation during final approach, though Russian officials stressed that this remained unconfirmed pending the results of the crash investigation.

## Aging Fleet Under Scrutiny

The crash has renewed scrutiny of aging Soviet-era and older Western aircraft still in operation among Russia's regional carriers. Aeroflot-Nord, a subsidiary of national carrier Aeroflot, has faced past criticism over its fleet maintenance and safety record, though the airline said in a statement that the aircraft involved had passed all required inspections.

"Our thoughts are with the families of all those who lost their lives," the airline said. "We are fully cooperating with investigators to determine what happened and will provide support to the families affected by this tragedy."

Russian President Dmitry Medvedev ordered a government commission to oversee the investigation and offered condolences to the victims' families, according to state media.

## Community in Mourning

In Perm, a city of just over one million people in Russia's Ural region, residents gathered near the crash site throughout the day, laying flowers and lighting candles in memory of the victims.

"This is a small city," one local resident said. "Almost everyone here knows someone who was affected, whether it was a relative, a friend, or someone from their workplace."

Authorities said recovery efforts at the crash site would continue for several days as investigators worked to identify victims and determine the exact sequence of events that led to the crash.

*This is a developing story. CNN will continue to update as more information becomes available.*
